name: TanStack AI Code Mode, QuickJS Bun driver (@tanstack/ai-isolate-quickjs-bun)

engine: Native QuickJS, compiled from the vendored C sources once per process by Bun's built-in TinyCC and called through bun:ffi; a new JSRuntime with its own heap and stack limits per execution, on the host's main thread
how_run: Under bun: createCodeModeTool({ driver: createQuickJSBunIsolateDriver(), tools: [lookup, failing] }).execute({ typescriptCode }); guest code calls external_lookup({id}).

source_notes.finding: Same Code Mode layer as the other TanStack drivers: external_<name> functions, TypeScript stubs from JSON Schema in the system prompt, and lazy tools behind discover_tools.

Each tool call creates a guest promise (vm.newPromise), runs the host binding asynchronously, and resolves the promise when it settles; the execution loop pumps pending jobs until the program settles or the deadline passes. Calls overlap, so P9 is parallel.

Native QuickJS in the Bun process via FFI, on the main thread. A QuickJS memory-safety bug would be a native bug in the host process, with no WASM boundary in between. The engine is compiled at runtime with TinyCC from C sources shipped in the npm package.
The only driver here with output and call-count caps, and the memory limit holds (P7 at 200 MB RSS, 104 MB hardened).
Guest stacks use the <code-mode> file name; no host stack is appended, unlike the QuickJS WASM driver.

surprises: Guest CPU loops block the whole Bun process for the full timeout (P6: 30 s), although docs call it the fastest sandbox for Bun.
Native QuickJS is compiled at first use with TinyCC from C source shipped in node_modules, which adds about 1.1 to 1.5 s to the first execution in each process.
This driver caps logs and tool calls, while the Node and QuickJS WASM drivers in the same project cap neither.
